blocks.text: The model is verified at three levels: unit benches per domain (`tests/`), system scenarios (`scripts/scenarios/scn_S*`) and the Phase 1 suite `run_phase1_tests`, which runs every case in a fresh MATLAB process and writes an HTML report. For the real robot the expected values of the tests were rewritten to follow from `P` (masses, gear ratio, current limits, number of cell groups), so the same tests now check the real-robot model.

The Full suite has 23 cases: the six Quick cases (power-up, RC driving, corrupted SBUS frames, front E-stop and two unit classes), the slope and link-loss scenarios, five test drives and nine unit classes. It ran twice on the four-motor model on 27 October 2026. The first run (report `phase1_full_20261027_180406`) used the first form of decision D64 (Ki 0.060 and a wider breakaway velocity of the brake). It failed S8a and test drive D2, where the engaged brakes diverged in ESTOP, and the standstill check of S6a / S6b; these findings gave the final D64 (section 4.3). It also showed that the battery bench still referenced the former 16-group pack ({tab:tab_unitfix}). The second run on the final model is the result below.
The Full suite ran on 27 October 2026 on the real-robot model: **17 of 23 cases PASS**, 2 FAIL, 4 KNOWN, 0 ERROR. The failing checks are explained in the next section.

blocks.text: Five checks fail on the final model ({tab:tab_dev}). Three are vehicle-level deviations accepted as known issues after the analysis of version 1.0 (user decision of 27 October 2026). The other two are unit tests whose causes lie outside the drive change; they are open items 11 and 12. U_mcu_platform also reports four known tests that still expect the stub units the MCU control units replaced (docs/STATUS.md 4.1).

blocks.text: With the IMU level calibration and TILT_WARN at 25 deg, the MCU estimate stays within about 1 deg of the true body pitch on the 20 deg ramp and TILT_WARN is never set ({fig:M44_s2_tilt_speed.png}a): the robot keeps its full speed limit and motor torque on its design slope. The remaining deviation is the ramp speed. With the belts at 0.80 m/s the tracks slip about 9.5 % at the tractive effort the 316 kg robot needs on 20 deg (0.44 of its weight), so the ground speed is 0.725 m/s against the 0.75 m/s criterion ({fig:M44_s2_tilt_speed.png}b, c). The slip is larger than in version 1.0 (about 7 %) because the track's relaxation length now matches the 0.75 m contact length (chapter 3). It depends on the estimated track size and the soil, and should be reviewed after the slope test (calibration test 2). During the 30 s hold on the ramp the engaged brakes keep the robot within 3 mm.

blocks.text: S6a / S6b: deceleration of the controlled stop

After the radio loss the MCU ramps the speed reference down at 1.0 m/s². On farm soil the tracks' motion resistance alone decelerates the robot at about 1.05 m/s², so the stop needs almost no braking ({fig:M45_s6_stop.png}c). The MCU feed-forward subtracts the inertia torque from the driving torque the speed loop is holding, and the ESC speed loop follows the reference slightly late; when it catches up, the ground deceleration peaks at 1.10 m/s² for about 0.2 s before it settles at the shaped 1.0 m/s² ({fig:M45_s6_stop.png}b). The robot is at standstill 1.12 s after the loss is detected (limit 1.5 s), never enters ESTOP, and its peak deceleration stays far below the 2 m/s² of the E-stop.

blocks.text: S8b (remote E-stop), whose mean deceleration was a known issue on the former robot, passes on the real-robot model, and so do S8a and test drive D2 with the elasto-plastic brake.
Unit tests on the four-motor model

Before the Full suite the affected unit classes were run on the four-motor model (153 tests). Most failures were not in the new drive itself: they were stale values from the change to the real robot that the new drive made visible. {tab:tab_unitfix} lists each finding, its cause and what was done.
